title: Evaluation of Bridges Collapsing in Omaha, Nebraska
text:
Executive Summary
This report evaluates the risk of a bridge collapsing in Omaha, Nebraska over the next five years. The goal is to help city decision makers understand current risks and identify actions that can reduce those risks.
Data from the National Bridge Inventory and federal traffic statistics were used to analyze bridge condition, age, and traffic levels. Information from the Nebraska Department of Transportation was used to provide additional context on maintenance. Risk was defined as a combination of the probability of failure and the consequences if a failure occurs.
The analysis shows that most bridges in Omaha are currently in fair to good condition. Out of 511 bridges, only 16 have a condition rating of 4 or below, meaning they may be at higher risk. Older bridges were more likely to have lower condition ratings, suggesting that deterioration over time is an important factor.
Traffic data shows that some bridges carry significantly higher volumes of vehicles than others. If one of these high traffic bridges were to fail, it would cause major disruptions and potential safety issues. Bridges with both low condition ratings and high traffic levels represent the greatest overall risk.
Overall, the risk of widespread bridge failure in Omaha is low. However, a small number of bridges require additional attention to prevent future problems.

Recommendations

Increase monitoring of older bridges with low condition ratings

Prioritize repairs for bridges in poorer condition

Continue regular inspections and maintenance

Focus on high-traffic bridges where failure would have the greatest impact

Taking these steps will help reduce the chance of bridge failure and limit the impact if a failure occurs.

title: 1  Introduction
text:
Bridge safety has become more of a concern in the United States after several bridge collapses in recent years. One example is the 2022 Pittsburgh bridge collapse (“Maintenance and Oversight Failures Led to 2022 Pittsburgh Bridge Collapse” n.d.). Events like this have caused cities to pay more attention to the condition and safety of their bridges.
In Omaha, bridges are important for everyday travel, especially on major roads like I-80 and routes that cross the Missouri River. If a bridge were to fail, it could lead to serious safety issues and major traffic problems.
The goal of this report is to estimate the risk of bridge collapse in Omaha over the next five years. This is done by analyzing bridge condition, age, and traffic levels using publicly available data. The results are meant to help the city identify higher risk bridges and understand what actions can be taken to reduce that risk.




“Maintenance and Oversight Failures Led to 2022 Pittsburgh Bridge Collapse.” n.d. Accessed April 17, 2026. https://www.ntsb.gov/news/press-releases/Pages/NR20240221.aspx.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.0.1 National Bridge Inventory
This analysis uses data from the National Bridge Inventory (NBI), filtered to include only bridges located in Douglas County, Nebraska, which also represents the Omaha area. Bridges with missing structural condition ratings were excluded from the analysis to avoid bias due to incomplete observations.
The main variables used include bridge age, deck rating, superstructure rating, substructure rating, lowest condition rating, and average daily traffic (ADT). Bridge age was calculated using the year built.
This analysis is descriptive and does not directly estimate the probability of bridge failure. Instead, bridge condition ratings are used as a proxy for relative failure risk. Bridges with lower condition ratings are treated as having higher risk, but this does not actually imply a specific probability of collapse.
To evaluate potential consequences of failure, average daily traffic was used as a measure of impact. Bridges with higher traffic volumes were considered to have greater potential consequences if a failure were to happen.
The overall goal of this approach is to identify bridges that may require additional monitoring or maintenance by combining information about structural condition and traffic levels.
The data comes from the Federal Highway Administration’s National Bridge Inventory (Federal Highway Administration 2025). This data set provides information about bridge age, condition ratings, location, and traffic levels. The main variables used from this data set are shown in Table 2.1.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.1 Selection of Relevant Variables
The variables used in this analysis are shown in Table 2.1, Table 2.2, and Table 2.3. The main variables include bridge age, deck rating, superstructure rating, substructure rating, lowest condition rating, bridge condition, and average daily traffic.
Bridge age was calculated using the year built.
Bridge condition was measured using deck, superstructure, and substructure ratings.
A bridge was classified as being in poorer condition if its lowest condition rating was 4 or below.

title: 2  Methods
text:
2.2 Evaluating Risk
To evaluate relative failure risk, bridges with lower condition ratings were treated as higher risk. To estimate the consequences of failure, average daily traffic was used as the measure of impact, with higher traffic indicating greater potential disruption.
Overall bridge risk was estimated using the formula:
Risk = Relative Failure Risk × Consequences of Failure
This approach was used to identify bridges that may require additional monitoring or maintenance, as discussed in Chapter 3.

These statistics indicate that most bridges are in acceptable condition, although a small subset may require additional attention.

Figure 3.2: Distribution of bridge condition ratings.
The distribution of condition ratings is shown in Figure 3.2, with most bridges falling into fair to good categories.
Out of the 511 bridges analyzed, 16 bridges have a condition rating of 4 or below, indicating poorer condition. This represents about 3% of all bridges, suggesting that most bridges are not currently in poor condition.
Traffic levels vary widely across bridges, with some carrying only a small number of vehicles per day and others exceeding 100,000 vehicles per day.

title: 3  Results
text:
3.2 Probability of Failure
The analysis shows that bridges with lower condition ratings have a higher risk of failure. Bridges with a lowest condition rating of 4 or below were identified as higher risk bridges.
The results also show that older bridges tend to have lower condition ratings. This suggests that bridge condition declines over time due to wear and usage. While most bridges are still in acceptable condition, there is a small group of bridges with lower ratings that may be at higher risk.

title: 3  Results
text:
3.3 Consequences of Failure








Figure 3.3: Relationship between bridge condition and traffic volume.





The relationship between bridge condition and traffic volume is shown in Figure 3.3. Bridges with both lower condition ratings and higher traffic volumes represent the highest overall risk, as they combine structural concern with greater potential impact.
Bridges with higher daily traffic volumes would result in the largest disruptions if a failure were to occur. Bridges that carry very high traffic volumes, especially on major roads like I-80, would have the greatest impact on transportation and public safety.
Information from NDOT (Nebraska Department of Transportation n.d.) provides context on maintenance and planned repairs, which may help reduce short-term risk.
These higher risk bridges are typically located along major transportation routes in Omaha. Since these routes are heavily used, a failure in these areas would cause major traffic disruptions and safety concerns.
These findings reinforce the importance of prioritizing bridges that combine both structural concerns and high usage.

3.3.1 Calculation of Bridge Risk
Overall bridge risk combines relative failure risk and the consequences of failure:
Risk = Relative Failure Risk × Consequence of Failure
As shown in Figure 3.4, bridge condition is used as a proxy for relative failure risk, and traffic data is used to estimate the impact of a failure.

title: 4  Conclusion
text:
The results show that most bridges in Omaha are in fair to good condition, with only 16 out of 511 bridges having a condition rating of 4 or below, which ends up being around 3%. This means the overall risk of a bridge collapse is low, but there are still some bridges that may need attention.
The data also shows that older bridges tend to have lower condition ratings, and bridges with higher traffic would cause the biggest problems if a failure occurred. Due to this, bridges that are both older and heavily used represent the highest risk.
Based on these findings, the city should focus on monitoring bridges with lower ratings more closely, prioritize repairs for these structures, and continue regular inspections. These actions would help reduce both the chance of failure and the impact if one occurs.
While more detailed data could improve these estimates in the future, focusing on maintenance and monitoring is currently the best way to reduce the risk of a bridge collapse in Omaha over the next five years.
